title: Anza's camp by the fine-water lake

place.label: Mountain Lake Park, near Lake St & 9th Ave

hook: In March 1776 Anza camped beside a lake 'of very fine water' and began planning the Presidio and Mission, on long-time Ohlone land.
story: Juan Bautista de Anza had led colonists hundreds of miles from Horcasitas, in today's Mexico, and left more than 200 of them waiting in Monterey. In late March 1776 his scouting party camped beside a lake near the mouth of the bay. He wrote that it was 'of very fine water', with running water, firewood and good grazing for cattle, though no timber 'even for barracks' [1]. A 1957 plaque in what is now Mountain Lake Park gives the date as March 27, 1776 [1]. On March 28, Anza and his chaplain, Father Pedro Font, left the camp and raised a cross on the cliff where Fort Point stands today. Over the next days they picked sites for the Presidio and the Mission [1]. The Presidio Trust notes that the Ohlone had lived in this area for more than a thousand years before the Spanish came [2]. Font described them as 'gentle Indians' who could fill 'a good and large mission', and historian Woody LaBounty points out what that meant. The Bay Area's Ohlone numbered about 10,000 when the Spanish arrived; sixty years later fewer than 200 were left [1]. The lake survives, smaller now, at the park's edge [2].

title: The racetrack under the Avenues

place.label: Bay District Racing Track site, 3rd Ave between Anza & Balboa

hook: Before the flats and bay windows, a one-mile racetrack filled these blocks. It once offered the biggest purse in America, and neighbours fought it for twenty years.
story: In August 1873 a group of the city's richest men leased 60 acres between First Avenue (today's Arguello), Fulton Street, Fifth Avenue and Point Lobos Road (today's Geary) for a one-mile track. The Bay District Racing Track opened in September 1874. On November 14 it ran a 'Great Race' with a $25,000 purse, the largest yet offered in America. The local favourite, 'Old Thad', lost to the Eastern mare Katie Pease, and the Chronicle's headline read 'THAD'S WATERLOO' [1]. Money trouble after the silver crash left the track without racing for three years. In 1890 Thomas Williams, then 30, brought it back with thoroughbreds and, from 1893, racing five days a week for months on end [1]. By then houses had crept up to its fence. Residents petitioned to reopen the streets the track had closed, and they complained about 'Beer Town', the saloons facing it on Fulton Street and Fifth Avenue [1]. The track closed on May 27, 1896. Two years later its empty ground became an army camp, and from 1902 builder Fernando Nelson covered it with homes [2].

title: The house that named a district

place.label: Site of George Turner Marsh's 'Richmond House', SE corner 12th Ave & Clement St

hook: An Australian-born dealer in Japanese art kept carrier pigeons, sent messages home by bird, and named his sand-dune estate after a suburb of Melbourne. The whole neighbourhood took the name.
story: George Turner Marsh was born near Melbourne in 1857. At 15, on his family's voyage to America, he begged to be left behind in Yokohama, and he stayed there until 1876. Back in San Francisco he opened what was probably the first Asian-art gallery in the United States [1]. He married Lucy Whiteside in 1880, and the couple built a home in the foggy 'Outside Lands'. It grew into a big estate at the southeast corner of 12th Avenue and Clement Street, with an ornamental stream, orchard and stables. The Newsom Brothers built a large house there in late 1886 [1]. Marsh rode to work downtown carrying pigeons. In the afternoon he sent one home to tell Lucy when he would be back and whether guests were coming for dinner [1]. He called the estate 'Richmond House', after the Melbourne suburb where he was born. In 1884 local property owners, tired of 'Outside Lands', chose 'Richmond' for the growing area, and in 1890 the supervisors made it official [1]. Some later accounts credit booster George R. Fletcher with the idea instead [1][2]. A 1917 ordinance renamed it 'Park-Presidio', but the new name never caught on. The city officially restored 'Richmond' in 2009 [1][2].

title: First Mass in a dance hall

place.label: Star of the Sea Church, 4420 Geary Blvd (parish began at 9th Ave & Geary)

hook: The Richmond's Irish dairy families had nowhere to worship. So on Easter Sunday 1887 they held Mass upstairs in Farrell's Dance Hall.
story: In the 1880s the land along Point Lobos Road was sand, fog and dairy ranches. Locals nicknamed it 'Pneumonia Gulch', and many of the ranchers were Irish [1]. Catholic families made the long trip to Old St. Mary's, or to the Holy Cross cemetery chapel on Eddy Street. In 1886, forty-one families decided they were 'strong enough' to support a church of their own [1]. The first Mass was said on Easter Sunday 1887 on the second floor of Farrell's Dance Hall at Ninth Avenue and Geary. Within a year the congregation had built a 500-seat wooden church for $10,000 [1]. The original Star of the Sea faced Eighth Avenue, behind the site of today's church. In the 1890s it was the only church near Point Lobos Avenue [2]. It became a full parish in 1894 under Father John P. Coyle, the first San Francisco-born man ordained a Catholic priest. Coyle led it through the 1906 earthquake and the growth that followed [1]. His successor, Father Philip O'Ryan from County Tipperary, opened the parish school with the Sisters of St. Joseph in 1909, with 137 children [1]. The present church dates from 1914 [1].

title: The French hospital built to stop contagion

place.label: French Hospital site, Geary Blvd between 5th & 6th Aves

hook: A mutual-aid society started by homesick French gold-seekers built a hospital out in the dunes. Each kind of disease got its own building, so patients could not infect one another.
story: The French Hospital began in December 1851 as La Société Française de Bienfaisance Mutuelle. Led by journalist Étienne Derbec, it set out to help French immigrants who came back from the mines sick, broke and unable to speak English. Its first home was a rented wooden house with 20 beds [1]. The society soon ran on dues-paying membership and moved several times. In the late 1880s it paid $48,000 for a full block on Point Lobos Road between Fifth and Sixth Avenues, surrounded by open land [1]. The chosen design, by M.G. Morin-Goustiaux working with M. Mooser, was unusual for its time. It separated diseases by type into pavilions set apart from one another, to stop contagion spreading from ward to ward [1]. The cornerstone was laid on February 25, 1894. A year later the 170-bed hospital opened with courts and gardens and one of the first nursing schools at a private hospital in the city [1]. The hospital moved to Point Lobos Road in 1895 [2]. A new building replaced it in 1963, and the site is now Kaiser Permanente's French Campus [2].

title: Seven thousand soldiers on the sand

place.label: Camp Merritt plaque, 695 2nd Ave at Cabrillo St

hook: In the summer of 1898 the old racetrack became a tent city of volunteers bound for the Philippines. Saloons sprang up, measles spread, and ten men never left.
story: After Dewey's victory at Manila Bay in May 1898, volunteers from Pennsylvania to Oregon poured into San Francisco to sail for the Philippines. The Presidio was short of water, so from May 18 white tents went up on the empty Bay District track, between today's Geary, Fulton, Arguello and Sixth Avenue [1]. The camp was named Camp Merritt, though General Wesley Merritt himself stayed at the Palace Hotel [1]. The Richmond Banner called the neighbourhood 'the liveliest part of the city'. It also warned mothers against letting daughters visit the camp without chaperones [1]. Thirteen new 'groggeries' opened, including 'The Maine' on First Avenue, before the city stopped issuing liquor licences [1]. Sand, fog, thin blankets and poor sanitation took their toll. Ten men died of measles, typhoid and other diseases [1]. The number of men is disputed: Western Neighborhoods Project says close to 7,000 camped in the Richmond, while the California State Military Museum gives 18,000 [1][2]. The camp was cleared by August 1898 [1]. In 1952, seven veterans unveiled a plaque at 695 Second Avenue. It went missing and was put back up in 2008 [1].

title: Shoot the Chutes on Fulton Street

place.label: Site of the Chutes amusement park, 10th Ave & Fulton St

hook: Boats that bounced and flipped, a zoo, a mirror maze and the Avenues' first moving pictures, all for a dime, just across from Golden Gate Park.
story: Early in the 1900s the Chutes amusement park sat just off D Street, now Fulton Street, at Tenth Avenue [1]. Its main ride sent boats down a steep flume into a pool. 'There was no safety device on those old Shoot-the-Chutes and those boats would literally go flying,' one man told the Western Neighborhoods Project. 'They flipped over all the time!' [1] The Chutes also showed some of the first films in the Avenues, before Fisher's opened on Clement Street in 1907. A Chronicle ad from March 21, 1904 promised moving pictures of boxers Britt and Young Corbett in training, a 'Cabaret de la Mort', 'animals from all climes in the zoo', a mystic mirror maze and a trip down the flume. Admission was 10 cents, or 5 cents for children [1]. The park did not last. In May 1910 builder Fernando Nelson bought the whole block and a half it had covered, on the east side of Tenth Avenue and between Cabrillo and Fulton from Tenth to Eleventh [2]. Over the next few years the Nelsons covered it with homes, including a half-timbered house at the northeast corner of Tenth and Fulton [2].

title: 'Only Caucasians' at Presidio Terrace
hook: San Francisco's first master-planned enclave sold electric streetlights, buried wires and a promise in print that no one who wasn't white could live there.
story: In 1905, Baldwin & Howell began building Presidio Terrace off Arguello Boulevard. It had 36 large lots around one private oval street, with electric streetlights, underground utilities and roads laid out for cars, all rare at the time [1][2]. After the 1906 fire, well-off families rebuilt here, in houses designed by leading architects including George Applegarth, Albert Farr and Julia Morgan [1]. The developer's 1906 advertisement made its main selling point plain: 'There is only one spot in San Francisco where only Caucasians are permitted to buy or lease real estate or where they may reside. That place is Presidio Terrace.' Its headline read 'The Japs Have Invaded The Western Addition' [3]. That was the same year the school board ordered Asian children segregated [3]. The builder Fernando Nelson bought a double lot in 1909 and built No. 30 there in 1910 [4]. Rules like this were declared unenforceable nationwide in 1948, when the Supreme Court decided Shelley v. Kraemer [3]. The gate still stands at the entrance on Arguello [3].

title: Carzonia: homes made from cable cars

place.label: Site of Carzonia apartments, California St at 5th Ave (strip between California & Cornwall)

hook: With the city short of housing after the 1906 fire, a Richmond doctor lined up ten old cable cars on his land and turned them into apartments.
story: After the 1906 earthquake and fire, thousands of San Franciscans needed somewhere to live, and the Richmond filled quickly. By November the Richmond Banner reported whole blocks of new houses selling before they were built [2]. Dr. Charles V. Cross, who lived on California Street at Fifth Avenue, came up with his own answer [1]. Copying the Carville streetcar colony in the Outer Sunset, he lined up ten old McAllister line cable cars on the narrow strip of his property between California and Cornwall Streets. He named them the 'Carzonia apartments' [1]. A fellow physician, Dr. S. Ward Moss, served as architect and added plumbing and electricity [1]. Neighbours worried the cars would look shabby. Cross promised that 'the cars will be transformed into artistic living apartments, surrounded with pretty flowers and will be attractive' [1]. He lived in one of the cars himself and had more applicants than cars before they were even finished [1]. Carzonia lasted less than four years. In early 1911 Cross put up a regular building on the land, and it still stands [1].

title: The builder with plans on an index card

place.label: Fernando Nelson homes, 4th-5th Aves between Balboa & Cabrillo

hook: Fernando Nelson carried his two house plans on a single index card and collected mortgage payments at the door. Hundreds of Inner Richmond homes are his.
story: In 1902 Fernando Nelson bought land on the old Bay District track, already graded and served by new water and sewer lines [1]. He built only when a buyer had signed up. His two floor plans, A and B, were printed on either side of an index card he carried in his pocket [1]. He often put the plumbing at the back so that a house could later be split into flats, and he often carried the buyer's mortgage himself, calling in person each month for the cash [1]. Look for his 'donuts', a row of jigsawed redwood circles above the front door [1]. After the 1906 quake the army took his lumber. By November the Richmond Banner reported he was building on the whole block between Fourth and Fifth Avenues, B and C Streets (now Balboa and Cabrillo), with houses 'sold before being built' [1]. In 1909 the Banner claimed he had put up a house every working day for six years. John Freeman's count is 246 buildings [1]. Nelson also set a San Francisco to Los Angeles driving record in November 1906 [1]. His family left the Richmond by 1916 [1].

title: The revolt against 'Spanish Town'

place.label: Arguello Boulevard (formerly First Avenue) at Clement St

hook: In 1909 the city tried to swap the numbered avenues for Spanish names from Arguello to Zamorano. The Richmond fought back, and a pirate joke helped end it.
story: In November 1909 a Street Naming Commission, trying to sort out mail muddled after the quake, proposed replacing every numbered avenue in the Richmond and Sunset with Spanish names in alphabetical order: Arguello, then Coronado, De Soto and on to Zamorano for 26th Avenue. Spanish saints would follow after that [1]. The Board of Supervisors approved it 12 to 5. Speakers from the Avenues called the names 'unpronounceable', and some said the city was 'selling out' to the Spain the country had just beaten in the Philippines. They said the district would be mocked as 'Spanish Town' [1]. The Richmond's improvement club organised petitions, and the commission backed down at a meeting in Richmond Hall on November 20 [1]. At one hearing a lawyer objected to naming First Avenue 'St. Francis Boulevard' because St. Francis Drake had been 'one of the very worst pirates'. The chairman reminded him that St. Francis of Assisi was a priest, and the room broke into laughter [1]. The numbered avenues stayed, but First Avenue became Arguello, and the lettered streets became Anza, Balboa and Cabrillo [1][2].

title: America's first big city-owned streetcars

place.label: Geary Blvd at Arguello Blvd (old cable car barn)

hook: Frustrated by a slow private cable line, the city refused to renew its franchise and built its own railway on Geary. Muni was born here in December 1912.
story: In the late 1800s the Geary Street, Park & Ocean Railroad ran cable cars out Geary to the Richmond on a franchise renewed each year. They kept a carbarn at Geary and Arguello, and its brickwork survives inside a later building [1]. The small cars ran at about six miles an hour. Progressive reformers wanted public ownership of utilities, and voters approved a bond for a city streetcar line in 1909, partly out of anger at the private United Railroads [1][2]. When the franchise ran out, the last cable car ran on May 5, 1912. Crews dug the cable machinery out of Geary and strung trolley wires overhead [1]. On December 28, 1912, Mayor James Rolph opened the Municipal Railway's first lines, the A and B, both on Geary [1]. SFMTA calls it the first major publicly owned, land-based transit agency in the United States [2]. The A turned at Tenth Avenue for Golden Gate Park, and the B went on towards the beach. A later C line turned at Second Avenue to reach California Street [1].

title: Post office, potatoes, then candy
hook: One Clement Street building went from post office to potato market to a sweet shop selling 'candy with a college education'.
story: After the 1906 earthquake, people moved into the Inner Richmond quickly, and the district needed a bigger post office. The building at 708 Clement Street went up in 1907 as branch post office Station M. Wagons unloaded mail on the Eighth Avenue side, and customers came in from Clement [1]. By August 1912 the neighbourhood had outgrown it again, and a bigger brick Station M opened at Tenth Avenue and Clement [1]. In 1918 former saloonkeeper John C. Jacobs opened the Pioneer Potato Market here, selling onions, potatoes, fruit and vegetables [1]. From 1921 to 1923 it was part of James O'Brien's candy factory, with a shop on the Clement Street side. O'Brien later moved to 506 Clement, the future home of Green Apple Books [1]. Then Ernest Wilson, a Stanford graduate who called his sweets 'the candy with a college education', opened a 'Confectaurant' here. It served ices, sodas, pastries and tea [1]. The vaulted ceiling probably dates from the O'Brien or Wilson years. Since 1984 it has been the Clement Street Bar & Grill [1].

title: San Francisco's first Carnegie library
hook: The steel magnate Andrew Carnegie's money built libraries across America. The first one San Francisco built with it went up in the Richmond, not downtown.
story: The Richmond got a library early. It was the fourth branch in the San Francisco Public Library system, opened in 1892 at 809 Point Lobos Avenue, now Geary, at Parker Avenue [1]. As the district grew after 1906, the city used a grant from Andrew Carnegie to build a proper branch on Ninth Avenue. It opened in 1914, the first library building in San Francisco paid for with Carnegie money [1]. Architects Bliss & Faville designed it in the Classical Revival style, in sandstone and reinforced concrete [2]. Six more Carnegie branches followed, in Chinatown, Golden Gate Valley, the Mission, Noe Valley, the Presidio and the Sunset, and all seven are still libraries [2]. The Richmond branch became San Francisco Landmark No. 247 after being nominated in December 2000 [1][2]. It reopened in 2009 after a seismic renovation, and today it carries the name of Senator Milton Marks [1].

title: Gracie Allen's age, solved by a yearbook
hook: Gracie Allen joked that the 1906 earthquake had destroyed her birth certificate. A Richmond schoolbook bought at an auction helped settle how old she was.
story: Comedian Gracie Allen, George Burns's partner, never gave her age straight. The joke went that the 1906 earthquake had destroyed her birth certificate, and Burns claimed he didn't know how old she was either [1][2]. Birth years given for her range from 1895 to 1906 [1][2]. Historian John Freeman went to Star of the Sea Grammar School in the late 1940s and had heard she was a former student. He won a Star of the Sea yearbook at auction. Its high-school class of 20 had four boys and one Grace Cecelia Allen [1]. The 1910 census showed her family living on Fourth Avenue in the Richmond District. That census wasn't much help on dates: in ten years, family members had aged only three to nine years [1]. Freeman compared her face with a 1914 Chronicle photo of her dancing and went back to the hard-to-read 1900 census. He concluded she was born on July 26, 1895, and graduated from Star of the Sea High School on June 19, 1914, a month before she turned 19 [1]. The Chronicle's list of famous Bay Area graduates also gives her as Star of the Sea, class of 1914 [3].

title: A Byzantine dome rises on Lake Street

place.label: Temple Emanu-El, 2 Lake St at Arguello Blvd

hook: Twenty years after the fire gutted its Sutter Street temple, the West's oldest Jewish congregation built a domed temple at the edge of the Richmond.
story: Congregation Emanu-El grew out of the Gold Rush. Its founders were mostly Bavarian Jewish merchants, and it was chartered in 1851 [3]. Its twin-spired Sutter Street temple was destroyed in April 1906. At first members patched it up within its old walls on a budget 'not to exceed $75,000' [1]. Two decades after the quake, the congregation finished a new temple at Arguello Boulevard and Lake Street, on the edge of the Richmond [1]. The Jewish Daily Bulletin listed the design team: the late architect Schnaittacher, the firm of Bakewell & Brown, and consulting architects Bernard Maybeck and G. Albert Lansburgh [2]. The style was 'Levantine', which the congregation described as a 'fusion of the architectural styles of Asia Minor, Palestine and the Mediterranean world' [1]. A fountain in the atrium recalls the ritual washing of ancient Jerusalem [1]. NoeHill notes that the dome was influenced by Hagia Sophia [4]. The temple was dedicated over three days, April 16 to 18, 1926, and Mayor James Rolph was among the speakers [2]. The full group was expected to cost $1,250,000 [2].
